faq.a: Toe extensors are also supplied by the deep peroneal branch, which is injured together with dorsiflexors, so both are weak.
faq.q: Why does foot drop not affect toe extension?

faq.a: Yes, if the cause is removed early and rehabilitation started; chronic compression may lead to permanent deficit.
faq.q: Can a common peroneal lesion recover fully?

faq.a: Not mandatory, but it prevents falls and contracture while the nerve recovers; a simple splint can be used if AFOs are unavailable.

exam: A patient with a plaster cast presents with new foot drop – what is your next step? — Check for cast tightness, remove or loosen it, and reassess motor function.

How would you differentiate a common peroneal nerve injury from a L5 radiculopathy? — Examine hip abduction (gluteus medius) and knee reflex; L5 radiculopathy shows reduced ankle reflex and hip weakness.
What are the most common causes of common peroneal nerve palsy in a rural East African hospital? — Trauma (fibular fracture), prolonged leg crossing, tight plaster, and tuberculous osteomyelitis.
A diabetic patient develops foot drop; what investigations are essential? — Clinical exam, bedside nerve conduction if possible, and blood glucose/HbA1c to assess metabolic contribution.
Why is steroid therapy contraindicated until infection is excluded? — Steroids suppress immunity and can worsen TB or bacterial osteomyelitis, leading to spread.

Explain the role of physiotherapy in nerve recovery. — Early active dorsiflexion exercises maintain muscle bulk, prevent contracture, and promote nerve regeneration through activity‑dependent plasticity.
What is the significance of a positive Tinel’s sign over the fibular neck? — It indicates nerve irritation or regeneration, supporting a peripheral compressive cause.
When would you refer for surgical decompression? — Persistent deficit >3 months despite conservative measures, or evidence of nerve entrapment on imaging.
ai.title: Common Peroneal (Fibular) Nerve Injury
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The common peroneal nerve is vulnerable at the fibular head, causing foot drop and sensory loss. Recognise causes, exam findings and management, especially where resources are limited.

b: Motor: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, peroneus longus/brevis
Sensory: lateral leg, dorsum of foot, 1st web space
sections.p: The common peroneal nerve branches from the sciatic nerve, wraps around the fibular neck and divides into deep and superficial branches. It supplies ankle dorsiflexion, eversion and sensation over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

b: Foot drop = inability to dorsiflex ankle; patient walks on toes
Eversion loss = foot turns inward (varus)
Sensory loss = numbness over lateral shin and dorsum
sections.p: Injury produces a characteristic foot drop and sensory patch. The lesion is usually peripheral, not central, and often reversible if identified early.

b: Trauma: fibular neck fracture, knee dislocation
Compression: tight plaster, prolonged squatting, leg crossing
Infection: TB or bacterial osteomyelitis of fibula
Systemic: diabetic neuropathy, HIV‑related neuropathy
sections.p: Common in low‑resource settings due to trauma, prolonged leg crossing, compression from casts, or infections such as tuberculous osteomyelitis of the fibula.

t.b: Confirms motor and sensory deficits; distinguishes peripheral from central causes
Shows reduced amplitude in peroneal motor response; if unavailable, rely on exam
Detects fracture or bony deformity causing compression
Identifies external compression or neuroma; not essential if unavailable
Evaluates soft‑tissue injury, occult fracture, or infection

b: Remove tight casts or splints; advise against prolonged leg crossing
Immobilise ankle in neutral with a splint to prevent contracture
Physiotherapy: active dorsiflexion exercises, ankle‑foot orthosis (AFO) if affordable
If infection: start anti‑TB regimen or appropriate antibiotics; avoid steroids until infection ruled out
Control diabetes, optimise HIV therapy, correct vitamin deficiencies
sections.p: Remove the offending cause, protect the joint, and start rehabilitation. Treat underlying infection or metabolic disease when present.

b: Ask: “Can you lift your foot off the bed?” – tests dorsiflexion
Test sensation with light touch over the dorsum of the foot
Check for Tinel’s sign over the fibular neck – tingling indicates nerve irritation
sections.p: Exam questions often test pattern recognition, differential diagnosis and immediate steps.

b: Assuming central cause without peripheral exam
Leaving a tight plaster in place for >2 weeks
Prescribing steroids before ruling out TB osteomyelitis
sections.p: Pitfalls include misattributing foot drop to stroke, missing a compressive cast, or delaying infection work‑up.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive weakness despite removal of compression
Severe pain, swelling or fever suggesting infection
